editorials.title: Silent crisis of our time
editorials.passage:
On June 5, I wrote an Op-Ed in this newspaper on depression and briefly touched upon its frequent companion ~ loneliness. Space did not permit me to explore what I believe is one of the most serious yet least discussed problems confronting contemporary society. Depression attracts attention because its consequences can be dramatic. Loneliness, by contrast, often hides behind closed doors, polite smiles, social-media posts, and the appearance of normalcy. 

Yet loneliness may be one of the defining afflictions of our age. In 2025, the World Health Organization reported that roughly one in six people worldwide experiences loneliness. It is no longer merely a private sorrow but a global public-health concern affecting young and old, affluent and poor, in crowded cities and remote villages alike. The paradox is striking. We possess more tools for instantaneous communication than any previous generation, yet rarely have so many people felt so isolated. 

We can reach someone across the world in seconds but may not know the person next door. We accumulate contacts, followers, and online “friends,” while longing for one human being with whom we can speak honestly. The problem is not new. In The Conquest of Happiness, Bertrand Russell argued that human beings flourish when their interests and affections extend beyond themselves. Friendship, family, community, and meaningful engagement are not decorative additions to life but part of its foundation. Russell understood that happiness and belonging are intertwined ~ a lesson of renewed urgency today. India now faces social changes that make belonging increasingly difficult. 

Urbanisation, migration, academic competition, demanding careers, and shrinking households have transformed traditional life. Young adults leave home for education or employment and find themselves in unfamiliar cities without dependable support. Older parents remain behind, sometimes separated from their children by thousands of kilometres. Research based on the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India found that more than a third of Indians aged sixty and above in its sample reported feeling lonely. That figure demands attention. India once possessed a powerful, if imperfect, defence against isolation: the joint family. 

Grandparents, parents, children, uncles, and aunts often lived beneath one roof or nearby. Such arrangements produced tensions and obligations; nostalgia should not obscure that reality. Yet they also created a network of daily interaction and care. A child rarely returned to an empty home, an elderly person usually had someone nearby, and sorrow could be shared rather than endured alone. It is important to distinguish loneliness from solitude. Loneliness is not being alone; it is the painful feeling that one’s relationships lack the closeness, understanding, or belonging one needs. 

A person may spend hours alone and feel peaceful and fulfilled. Another may sit among relatives, attend parties, or work in an office and still feel profoundly lonely. Solitude can be nourishing; loneliness is felt as an absence. Some of India’s greatest figures understood that absence long before psychologists began measuring it. Rabindranath Tagore repeatedly explored loneliness, longing, loss, and the search for human connection. Despite international fame, he was no stranger to grief. The deaths of his wife, children, and other loved ones left deep emotional scars. Yet from sorrow he created poetry, music, and literature of extraordinary beauty. 

His work reminds us that loneliness is not a personal failure but a universal human experience. Jawaharlal Nehru likewise wrote of loneliness. During imprisonment and throughout much of his public life, he reflected upon not fully belonging. Educated in England yet deeply bound to India, he sometimes seemed caught between cultural worlds. His experience reminds us that loneliness can arise not only from physical separation but from cultural homelessness ~ the feeling of being at home everywhere and nowhere. Tagore and Nehru illustrate an important truth: loneliness is not cured by fame, power, or public admiration. 

One may be known by millions and still feel unknown. The history of Indian cinema offers equally poignant examples. Few artists captured isolation more powerfully than Guru Dutt. Pyaasa and Kaagaz Ke Phool remain haunting explorations of alienation, rejection, and the longing to be understood. Meena Kumari, adored by millions as the “Tragedy Queen,” gave voice to her private sorrow through poetry. Sanjeev Kumar, one of Hindi cinema’s most gifted actors, achieved immense professional success but, by many accounts, struggled with loneliness in his personal life. 

Their stories remind us that admiration is not intimacy, and applause is not companionship. The West offers similarly poignant examples. Vincent van Gogh’s letters reveal a man who longed for affection and companionship while enduring rejection and emotional isolation. Ludwig van Beethoven’s advancing deafness gradually excluded him from the social world he desperately needed, leaving him unable to participate fully in ordinary conversation. Marilyn Monroe, desired and admired by millions, appeared to struggle with the painful suspicion that the public loved her glamorous image without truly knowing the woman behind it. 

A painter, a composer, and a film star ~ their careers could scarcely have been more different, yet loneliness entered each of their lives. These are only three examples. There are many others whose names alone could fill this page, all bearing witness to the same unsettling truth: public recognition can never substitute for private belonging. Modern technology has introduced a troubling new dimension. Social media promises connection but frequently produces comparison. We encounter carefully curated images of other people’s holidays, achievements, friendships, marriages, and apparently flawless lives. 

Comparing their polished exteriors with our unedited interiors can leave us feeling inadequate and excluded. Meanwhile, the habits of digital communication may gradually erode the patience required for deeper relationships. Technology can sustain affection across continents and offer solace to isolated people. The danger arises when digital contact replaces human relationships. A text, emoji, or social-media “like” cannot replace heartfelt conversation or a friend’s dependable presence. Loneliness matters because its effects extend far beyond emotional discomfort. 

The World Health Organization links chronic loneliness and social isolation with depression, anxiety, heart disease, stroke, cognitive decline, and premature death. The lonely person may nevertheless continue to work, care for a family, attend social occasions, and appear perfectly well. Because loneliness leaves no obvious physical mark, people around them may never recognize the depth of their distress. There is no single remedy. Loneliness cannot be cured by an app, a pill, or a government programme alone. Meaningful connection requires time, effort, vulnerability, and presence. It also requires the courage to admit that we need other people. 

In a culture that celebrates self-sufficiency, such an admission is sometimes treated as weakness. It is nothing of the sort. The need to love and be loved is among the most fundamental facts of being human. Government nevertheless has a role. Public policy can support community centres, parks, libraries, senior programmes, public transport, mental-health services, and neighbourhood activities that bring people together. Schools can teach children how to listen, cooperate, and recognize distress. Workplaces can cultivate humane relationships rather than treating employees merely as units of productivity. Doctors should also ask patients, especially older adults, about social isolation. 

But institutions cannot do everything. Families must sometimes choose conversation over screens. Neighbours must rediscover the practice of noticing one another. We should telephone ageing parents, visit a bereaved relative, invite an isolated colleague for tea, and ask a struggling friend how he or she is really doing. Most importantly, we must remain long enough to hear the answer. What seems to us a small gesture may become someone else’s lifeline. Mother Teresa often spoke of the terrible poverty of feeling unwanted, unloved, and uncared for. 

That insight speaks directly to our age. The loneliness epidemic is not merely a psychological or medical challenge; it is a moral and social one. It asks whether, amid speed, distraction, and personal ambition, we are still willing to make room in our lives for one another. No technological invention can cure the human longing to be known, valued, and loved. The deepest remedies remain simple and timeless: listening without impatience, visiting without obligation, speaking with kindness, and offering our undivided presence. 

These gestures appear ordinary, but they are the threads from which companionship, community, and a humane society are woven. Loneliness seldom announces itself loudly. It lives in empty apartments, nursing homes, trains, and within those who seem to possess everything. We cannot eliminate loneliness, but we can ensure that fewer people endure it unnoticed. The answer begins when we pause, reach out, and offer a person the human assurance: you are seen, you are valued, and you are not alone. 

(The writer is professor emeritus at Loyola Marymount University, Los Angeles)

editorials.title: A birth year can’t be a worldview
editorials.passage:
Newsrooms have found a new noun and cannot put it down: Gen Z, pronounced as if it were a party with a leader, a manifesto, a whip and a press secretary. Anchors deploy it the way they once deployed “the youth”. Politicians use it the way they use “the people”. Reporters slap it on whoever is holding a placard this week and call the segment done. Jantar Mantar was filled by mid-July. 

Students sat in protest over a leaked examination, a cancelled NEET, a retest forced on millions, and a minister who simply would not go. On 20 July, a mass of people of all hues tried to walk towards Parliament. Police responded with tear gas and batons. Five days later, Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. This was the first cabinet exit in twelve years, extracted by street pressure and resolute determination. Then came the late-night Reels, the sudden “friends”, and, from the Red Fort on 15 August, a new phrase: dimaagi naxal. After the Jantar Mantar protests, it is impossible to watch television or YouTube, or to read a newspaper or a magazine, without being inundated with references to Gen Z. In truth, the commentary and so - called analysis that followed did two predictable things, and both were wrong. 

It read the sit-in as a generational uprising. It read the phrase as either a surgical strike on ideology or an attack on thought itself. In both cases, it mistook a demographic category for mindset. A protest is a fact about a demand or a grievance. A birth year is a fact about demography. A security label is a fact about how power prefers to categorise its critics. Today, everyone treats a demographic as a worldview, yet nothing could be further from the truth. Two people born in 2003 can leave the same decade with opposing politics. One sits at Jantar Mantar. One is in a coaching centre, preparing for the very exam being contested. One thinks the protesters are entitled. 

One cannot place Jantar Mantar on a map. All of them are Gen Z. None is more authentically Gen Z than the others. The cohort supplied the timeline. It did not dictate the mindset. We already know this, because we apply it correctly everywhere except in the present. Nobody treats “Boomer” as a single stance on the Emergency, liberalisation, caste or capital. The label survives as shorthand for age. It is not mistaken for a programme. Gen Z gets no such courtesy, because Gen Z is new, loud and convenient. A protest makes for cleaner copy if you can call it a rising. 

A Red Fort coinage makes for cleaner copy if you can call it either fascism or foresight. Both readings flatten what actually happened. Students sat in against a specific, documentable failure: an examination system that unscrupulous elements had learned to game. Some came from small towns, some from universities, and some from families who had spent years of savings on coaching for a paper whose integrity had just been publicly gutted. Their unity was centred on one grievance, held together by shared circumstance, not by shared ideology. When the minister resigned, the coalition loosened. Compensation was promised to the families of students who had die d by suicide following the cancellation. Cases against protesters were to be withdrawn. 

Broader exam reform was set aside for later talks. An ideological movement does not, more or less, dissolve the moment it wins one scalp. This one did. That alone should have told commentators what kind of event they were watching. The Instagram turn was not a conversation with a generation. It was an attempt to borrow the tone of the platforms protesters already inhabited, including selfie angles, Reels, and the repeated address “friends”, without first addressing the demand that had put them on the street. The reception was unkind because performance reads as exactly that. “We’re not friends” was not trolling; it was the iteration of a fact. 

You cannot use make-believe and call it intimacy. This was the outreach. Then came the attack. Standing on the ramparts of the Red Fort, built ironically by the fifth Mughal Emperor, Shah Jahan, the Prime Minister declared that armed Naxalism was breathing its last. What remained were dimaagi naxals: people with a Maoist mindset who had once sat in corridors and committees and were still seeking opportunities to promote violence and anarchy, a thinly veiled reference to the principal opposition party and the bureaucrats in their governments. 

Then came the call to action: citizens must identify and isolate them so the young could be steered into the mainstream of development. The term did not arrive from nowhere. It continues a longer series, including urban naxal, tukde-tukde gang, andolanjeevi, that seeks to draw a line between legitimate criticism and what the establishment frames as ideological subversion. After a claimed success against the armed phase, the residual threat was recast as intellectual. The honest defence deserves to be stated before it is tested. Union minister Kiren Rijiju said the phrase was not aimed at the opposition as a class. 

He said it named those who support Maoists and reject the Constitution; those who stand with separatists and with Article 370; and those who talk of cutting the chicken’s neck and separating the North-East. On that reading, the term is preventive: isolate residual ideology before it again influences institutions or romanticises disruption and makes it mainstream That appeared to be a coherent justification garbed in the robes of national security. What happened after was entirely another story. A label functions as a policy only if it is narrow enough to name a specific type of misconduct. Once it becomes conceptually ambiguous, it invites ridicule. Senior opposition figures declared themselves proud to be dimaagi naxals. 

Satirical accounts appeared within a day. An insult coined to isolate became, for a section of the online public, a membership card. That is not because an age cohort holds a Maoist brief. It is because a category that cannot distinguish a student furious about a leaked paper from a person who rejects the Constitution will be seized by both, and by everyone in between who enjoys watching a coined phrase rebound conclusively on its author. The error runs in both directions. You cannot treat every twenty-two-yearold at Jantar Mantar as the vanguard of a new politics, nor can you treat every critic of the phrase as a Maoist. Both reduce a person to a type and then treat the type as proof. 

Report the protest as a protest: a coalition of the specifically aggrieved who wanted a compromised exam system fixed, some of them young. Report the outreach as outreach: a botched attempt to sound familiar after previously alienating yourself. Report the speech as a speech and draw your inferences about what was said and what was meant. Modi did not suddenly become clumsy. He applied a method that has worked in older media and hierarchical mobilisation to a moment that rewards precision over atmosphere. 

A grievance is not a mindset or an ideology. A shared birth year does not indicate homogeneity. A generation is not a movement. Listening to people carry on about Gen Z, it seems they believe all three to be gospel truth. We already know this about every cohort except the one on the streets. No Boomer was ever the same. No member of Gen Z ever was either. And not every mind that objects is a Naxal, dimaagi or otherwise. 

(The writer is a Mumbai-based consultant)

editorials.title: Putin’s Trap
editorials.passage:
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s greatest problem may no longer be winning the war in Ukraine. It may be finding a way to stop it. More than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion, neither side has secured a decisive military breakthrough. Ukraine has survived predictions of collapse and increasingly demonstrated its ability to carry the war into Russia through long-range drone strikes. 

Moscow, meanwhile, retains vastly greater resources and continues to grind forward at enormous human cost, but without achieving the strategic victory that would justify the sacrifice. For Putin, this is an increasingly dangerous equilibrium. A compromise that leaves Ukraine outside Russian control and fails to deliver the territorial objectives for which he launched the invasion could look less like peace than an admission of failure. The Kremlin’s predicament is therefore not conventional military weakness. Russia remains a formidable power, with a large defence-industrial base, extensive manpower and the capacity to sustain repression. 

Its economy has adapted better than many Western forecasts anticipated. But strength does not automatically produce strategic success. Russia is powerful enough to continue the war, yet seemingly unable to end it decisively on its preferred terms. That combination creates an incentive to escalate. The most immediate danger is likely to be Ukraine. Another brutal winter campaign against electricity generation, heating and civilian infrastructure could be accompanied by intensified offensives and fresh recruitment. Reports that Moscow may seek hundreds of thousands of additional troops suggest that the Kremlin sees manpower, rather than political compromise, as the answer to stalemate. 

Yet escalation may not stop at Ukraine’s borders. Russia has already been accused by European governments of engaging in sabotage, cyber operations and other forms of hostile activity against countries supporting Kyiv. The logic is obvious: if direct confrontation with NATO remains too dangerous, pressure can instead be applied below the threshold of war. That makes Europe vulnerable to a different kind of conflict ~ one without a declaration of war. Attacks on infrastructure, disruption of transport, cyber sabotage, disinformation and mysterious security incidents can impose costs while preserving ambiguity. The danger lies precisely in miscalculation. 

A campaign designed to intimidate NATO could eventually trigger the collective response Moscow wishes to avoid. Putin's dilemma is rooted in the nature of personalised rule. Democratic leaders can lose elections and alter policy. Autocrats who have personalised a war cannot easily separate their own political survival from its outcome. The longer the conflict continues, the more difficult compromise becomes because the costs incurred demand an even larger justification. 

This does not mean Russia is about to attack NATO or that Putin has abandoned rational calculation. On the contrary, the greater likelihood is calibrated escalation: more violence in Ukraine, greater repression at home and more aggressive pressure on the West’s political and economic vulnerabilities. But calibrated escalation has a fatal weakness. Every new step creates consequences that cannot be fully controlled. Putin may still have many options. His problem is that increasingly none of them offer a clean exit.

editorials.title: Reality Check
editorials.passage:
India’s latest GDP growth figure has delivered precisely the kind of political dividend that impressive headline numbers are meant to produce. At a time when the Narendra Modi government faces uncomfortable questions about unemployment, weak private investment and uneven consumption, rapid economic growth offers a powerful counter-narrative. But the celebration surrounding the number risks obscuring a more important question: what, exactly, is India measuring? 

The controversy over the revised GDP series should not be reduced to a predictable contest between government triumphalism and opposition scepticism. Statistical methodologies require periodic revision. Economies change, new industries emerge and old datasets become inadequate. A failure to update national accounts would itself undermine credibility. If the new methodology genuinely captures economic activity more accurately, its introduction is justified. Yet methodological improvement does not absolve policymakers of the responsibility to explain its consequences clearly. 

When revisions substantially alter estimates of the economy's earlier size, comparisons with subsequent years become inherently more complicated. A spectacular growth rate may reflect genuine acceleration while also benefiting from a recalibrated statistical baseline. Both propositions can simultaneously be true. That distinction matters because GDP has increasingly become a political instrument. The more fundamental issue, however, lies beyond the statistical dispute. Economic growth must eventually become visible in the lives of citizens. India’s paradox remains striking. 

An economy supposedly expanding at one of the fastest rates among major nations continues to struggle with youth employment. Private investment, though showing encouraging signs of revival, remains uneven. Foreign direct investment has not matched the expectations generated by India’s geopolitical and demographic advantages. These are not minor qualifications to an otherwise successful story. They are tests of whether growth is sufficiently broad-based to sustain itself. The composition of the expansion is equally important. Tax cuts, lower interest rates and government spending can stimulate activity, but their effects are not permanent. 

Export growth aided by a weaker rupee may improve competitiveness, but currency depreciation also makes imported energy and industrial inputs more expensive. India’s rapid diversification of energy supplies during the West Asia crisis demonstrated administrative agility, yet the country’s dependence on imported crude remains a structural vulnerability. Then comes the monsoon. Weak rainfall threatens agricultural output, rural incomes and food prices, potentially creating the uncomfortable combination of slower consumption and higher inflation. If inflationary pressures force the Reserve Bank of India to tighten monetary policy, the very investment recovery now being celebrated could face fresh headwinds. 

None of this means India’s growth is illusory. There are genuine strengths: infrastructure investment, manufacturing expansion, digitalisation and an increasingly important role in global supply chains. But confidence in an economy cannot rest indefinitely on one quarterly number, however impressive. The ultimate verdict on India’s growth will not come from statistical revisions or political slogans. It will come from whether expansion creates productive jobs, attracts sustained private capital and raises incomes beyond the already prosperous sections of society. Until then, the most sensible response to a spectacular GDP figure is neither disbelief nor euphoria, but scrutiny.

editorials.title: Digital divides
editorials.passage:
When did you last visit the post office? I last went over two years ago. Yet before the advent of courier services, and even more of email, WhatsApp and mobile banking, the post office was a hub of the locality. We would queue for hours to send a money order or registered letter, or pay our telephone bill. As with any sarkari institution, it had a penumbra of informal operators. Prominent among them was the composite letter writer, form filler and parcel packer. For those who could not read and write, he would write and address letters (or even read out incoming ones), fill in money order forms, and seal banknotes in insured packets for migrant workers to send home. The inland remittance economy, the lifeline of the working poor, would have collapsed if this functionary (himself often a migrant worker) did not exist.

Educated persons seldom availed of his services. At most, they might ask him to sew up a cloth parcel. This was among the endless silent barriers between the literate and the illiterate, the washed and the unwashed. The privileged could stride into the post office and conduct their business directly. The unprivileged needed this guide and intercessor.

Far fewer people are illiterate today, and far fewer use the postal services. The letter writer and form filler may be a dying profession. But we may still wonder how many neo-literates can fill up the average form. This does not necessarily reflect on their education, as Indian forms pose formidable challenges. They are needlessly long and complicated, and phrased in various shades of goobledygook. Indian-language versions are often more opaque than the original English, being over-literally translated from the latter instead of following the bent of their own tongue. Highly educated people are often stumped by them. For the average citizen, especially the poorly educated and socially insecure, official paperwork is an instrument of State tyranny.

Hence the ubiquitous middleman or facilitator, from the harmless letter writer to the mediator of applications and speed money. They include the people who arrange your car tax payment or income tax return.

The coming of the computer is thought to have ended the tyranny of the middleman. The claim is not entirely untrue. Many processes, from paying vehicle tax to buying a train ticket, can now be done online, neatly and quickly. Where the middleman was never an issue, as in retail banking, we can manage our finances in a faster and allegedly foolproof way, though many will question that last adjective.

But at another level, computerisation has spawned new dangers and deterrents that have hurt many people and bewildered countless others. The biggest single group might be elderly people who received an exemplary education in their youth but have been left behind by the computer revolution. They are wary even of a UPI payment app or an eminently user-friendly site like the Indian Railways’ booking portal.

Needless to say, not all the elderly fall in this category. We should not infantilise their tribe (to which I myself belong). A colleague of mine, an expert in scholarly computation, is furious because the State Bank refuses to allow her a netbanking account. It would be good to know how many seniors share either her stand or her expertise. Many others clearly would not venture on such a course.

The resistance is at two levels. One is the lack of technical confidence even for simple tasks. The other is a gut distrust of the Establishment. After a lifetime of queueing and bribing for railway berths, they cannot view the online portal as either truthful or reliable. They are convinced it is a front for backdoor bookings. Being ourselves conditioned to think that way of all public amenities, how many of us can demur with full conviction, even if we don’t really agree?

In a word, distrust of digital systems as the behemoth of arbitrary rule has spread beyond the educationally deprived. Being also economically deprived as a rule, the latter see fintech as a ploy of the exploiting classes. Today, the distrust has spread to a sizeable section of educated people. We do not always recognise how the digital divide cuts through class divisions. It does not merely exclude the poor. It also disempowers a section of society enjoying some degree of power and security through education, affluence or social affinity.

These are people supremely at ease with the world of pen, paper and print. Now they find the goal posts have shifted to a distance they cannot cover. Technology lies like a dragon between them and their money or travel or medical treatment. Nothing will convince them that the dragon is actually for their protection. Why should they think so, amid daily reports of online scams?

The young may be as distrustful of the world, but they were born to the technology and attuned to it. Where the malign human imagination comes into play, they are as vulnerable as their elders. Not long ago, a young Bangalore techie was cheated out of crores under threat of ‘digital arrest’. But unlike their seniors, they are not overfaced by the technology itself. They are naturally conditioned to the rhythm and ethos of an electronically mediated society. If they fall prey, it is through over-familiarity and over-confidence with the medium.

Hence the most piquant of the new disruptions in the electronic age: traditional worldly wisdom counts for less than ever before. The young have as much, if not more, to teach the old as the other way around — and I am not talking only about technology. Yet the old order exists, and for good and ill, largely controls the world. Will things change when those now young grow old? Or will they fall into the timeworn pattern? The elderly will not be there to see. For now, they can only think of reversing the familiar maxim to ‘If age knew, if youth could.’

Sukanta Chaudhuri is Professor Emeritus, Jadavpur University

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Chinese entrepreneur turns scratching an itch into 100,000 yuan business
editorials.passage:
Sir — An itch on an unreachable spot on one’s back may be one of the most uncomfortable feelings of life. But is it worth 100,000 yuan? In China, an entrepreneur has turned the simple act of scratching an itch into a business and is earning an estimated 14 lakh rupees per month from it. A one-hour-long session costs about 300 yuan or Rs 4,200. This might seem like something to laugh at but it highlights a crucial problem. Getting an unreachable itch scratched is usually something one asks a close friend or relative to do. But in an increasingly lonely world, even such an intimate act has to be outsourced at a cost.

Sir — The food safety drive being undertaken by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation is laudable (“KMC tightens food safety checks”, Sept 4). The amount of rotten, stale and adulterated fish, meat and sweets being recovered from the storage facilities of various restaurants, eateries, canteens, and food markets at different locations in the city is shocking. Food safety should be a priority of the state government, alongside education, health, drinking water and so on. It must also be ensured that during strict inspections, food safety is not compromised by under-the-table transactions.

Sir — Reports of stale food, adulterated eatables and unlicensed food items being sold in large quantities appear frequently in the media. This is in spite of the fact that there are departments staffed with qualified officials to ensure strict adherence to specified norms. But the absence of regular checks leaves people vulnerable to serious health risks.

A.G. Rajmohan, Andhra Pradesh

Sir — Rumours and reports often circulate about rackets collecting animal carcasses from municipal dumps to sell to restaurants. Yet, food safety drives like the one being undertaken now are not regular affairs. If regulatory oversight was periodic, transgressions would not take place. To truly deter offenders who violate food safety standards, the authority must enforce strict penalties with absolute regularity.

Sir — Sanjoy Hazarika’s article, “Nature’s fury” (Sept 2), highlights the unprecedented devastation in Assam. While governments aggressively track ghuspaithiyas , they ignore the recurring floods that drown Assam and North Bihar every monsoon. To break this cycle, fiscal policy must evolve. A dual-budget framework is a must: a National Climate Resilience Fund for year-round engineering solutions and an emergency relief fund. Policy measures should focus on long-term safety mechanisms.

Sir — The recent catastrophic floods in Assam devastated the lives of many migrant workers, leaving them entirely destitute. Two dairy farmers, Rishiram and Vinod, for example lost their livelihoods after the sudden surge of water submerged both their fields and homes. The disaster destroyed their crops, washed away their cattle, and swept away their vehicles, including motorbikes and scooters, leaving them in a truly desperate situation. The government must immediately provide rehabilitation and support to workers like them. Non-governmental organisations need to help them rebuild their lives after this devastating incident.

Sir — Early warning systems are desperately needed around the world to save thousands of lives from natural disasters aggravated by climate change. The devastating floods in Assam and the flash floods in Nepal recently destroyed entire communities and the livelihoods of many, not to mention took hundreds of lives. In Nepal, the water’s sheer force and swirling motion even caused heavy concrete structures to float away like straw. Northeastern states in India will face a similar predicament unless ameliorative steps are taken.

Sir — Gloria Steinem, a prolific writer and one of the best-known faces of the women’s liberation movement, died last week at the age of 92. She was a journalist, activist, political organiser, and speaker. She battled alongside other stalwarts of the movement for the Equal Rights Amendment in the United States of America, while advocating for reproductive freedom, raising awareness about violence against women, and co-founding Ms. , a magazine run and staffed entirely by women.

Sir — The death of Gloria Steinem, an iconic American writer and a leading light of second-wave feminism, marks the end of an era of the American women’s liberation movement. Her relentless campaigns redefined women’s rights globally. She was also involved in the Vinoba Bhave Bhoodan movement in India.

editorials.title: Honour minus rights
editorials.passage:
This year's budget by the Bengal government raised the monthly 'honorarium' of anganwadi workers by Rs 5,000. Yet, no one chose to think about what an honorarium is, and why it is not called a salary.

The word has a long and rich history. It originally comes from the Roman honorarium , a gift given not out of obligation but out of esteem — for instance, to the grammarian who had corrected your Latin or to the poet who had written your epitaph. An honorarium is something that is not legally binding by nature. It suggests that one's actions have been met with thankfulness and not with a sense of obligation; in other words, it is an act of generosity rather than a claim to a right. Thus, when the government refers to what it pays anganwadi workers as an honorarium, it is not only arbitrarily determining the value of their work but is also making a philosophical statement about the nature of the work.

According to government data, India's anganwadi and ASHA workforce numbers approximately 34 lakh: 13.48 lakh anganwadi workers and 10.23 lakh anganwadi helpers (ministry of women and child development data, as of December 2023), and 10.47 lakh ASHA workers. These workers form the delivery team through which the Indian government fulfils its constitutional promise under Article 47 to improve nutrition and public health. They administer vaccines to babies, provide guidance to mothers who are breastfeeding, maintain nutrition records for households, and conduct schooling for young children who are not familiar with private schools. In 2022, the Supreme Court emphasised that it could not accept that these workers be given part-time, voluntary status. They, the court argued, are doing full-time jobs. The Bengal budget also recognises that their services are vital. However, the term, 'employee', is still missing on paper.

There is something particular, and peculiarly Indian, about this arrangement. Almost the entire frontline workforce of the country's child nutrition and primary healthcare systems is female. All anganwadi workers are women. All ASHA workers are women. Women also do the mid-day meal cooking. The irony is that they are all paid honorariums; in other words, they are considered volunteers. Reetika Khera, an economist who has widely researched and written on these schemes, has framed this as such: a gendered division of labour whereby care work is seen as something women are naturally good at and, hence, is not work in the legal or economic sense.

Bengal's Rs 5,000 hike is a raise. However, a raise that takes place within an honorarium framework is a raise without rights. The anganwadi worker gets more money, but still does not have any legal recourse, is not entitled to a minimum wage floor, does not have job security, and cannot claim social protection. The Code on Wages, 2019 states that an employee is a person who is working "on wages" for "hire or reward". By calling the anganwadi workers' remuneration an honorarium, the State continues to evade this definition and, consequently, every duty that comes with it.

It is worth recalling what Bengal's budget also said: that these workers supply "vital services": vital services that are carried out every day, in both villages and city slums, primarily by women who have no employment status, no minimum wages, no EPF or ESI, not even the right to challenge their removal before a labour tribunal. The state honours them generously. It is the recognition it withholds.

editorials.title: Unsafe bite: Editorial on food adulteration in India and culture of impunity
editorials.passage:
Food adulteration in India is a pressing issue affecting millions of citizens. Nearly one in five food samples tested across the country was found to be non-conforming to mandated safety standards in 2025-26: significantly, only 4.8% of such violations ended in convictions. Moreover, of the 8.86 lakh samples analysed between 2021-22 and 2025-26, about 20% were found to be adulterated: only 3.3% of these established violations resulted in convictions. There is also a wide disparity among states when it comes to conviction rates. Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan accounted for 62.5% of all adulterated samples in 2025-2026 but only around 19% of convictions. Tamil Nadu, on the other hand, recorded not only the highest number of samples tested but also one of the best rates of convictions. Astonishingly, several states recorded no convictions at all. Such administrative apathy is what assures wrongdoers of impunity. Staple food items are repeatedly found adulterated with detergent, urea, starch, synthetic colours, cheap oils and industrial chemicals. But the trade survives because, reports suggest, small manufacturing units operate under local political protection in exchange for bribes. West Bengal’s ongoing inspection drive across restaurants, sweet shops and other eateries shows that even if food is not adulterated at the source, it can become dangerous for consumption during improper storage.

This does not mean that India does not have extensive food safety laws. The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, provides for licensing, inspection, seizure, prosecution and graded punishment; the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, permits compensation; and Sections 274 and 275 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita criminalise adulteration and the sale of noxious food. Yet fines remain as low as Rs 1,000, encouraging repeat offences, while understaffed departments — 91 of its 105 sanctioned food safety posts in Bihar are vacant — inadequate laboratories, delayed reports and defective sampling allow prosecutions to collapse. The failure extends to the Public Distribution System on which millions of poorer citizens depend. Foodgrain moves through a fragmented supply chain without adequate storage or systematic inspection or reliable quality control. India needs district-level laboratories, uniform sampling procedures, batch testing of high-risk foods, mandatory traceability, publicly accessible inspection results and penalties linked to turnover and repeated violations. Countries with stronger food-safety systems rely on continuous surveillance, effective recalls and clear responsibility across the supply chain. Deliberate toxic adulteration should invite swift criminal prosecution, and officials who suppress violations should face personal liability. Adulteration will continue until institutional weaknesses and culpability are eradicated.

editorials.title: Weaponised: Editorial on maternity leave and workplace discrimination
editorials.passage:
Does the right to maternity leave sit uneasily with India’s workplaces? The Delhi High Court recently had to reiterate a basic principle: pregnancy and maternity leave cannot be grounds for demotion at work for employees. For women returning from maternity leave, the transition can bring significant physical, emotional and professional challenges. For instance, Rakhi Bisht, the petitioner in the above mentioned case, found herself redesignated to a substantially inferior role. Justice Sachin Datta of the Delhi High Court has held that maternity leave cannot, under any circumstance, become a source of ignominy at the workplace. The judgment is significant because it identifies an insidious form of discrimination: the weaponising of maternity leave — a statutory right — against women workers. Law grants women maternity leave as a right. The workplace, however, often treats the exercise of that right as a professional liability.

A woman should not have to be apprehensive that taking legally sanctioned leave will cost her a promotion, a meaningful role, or be a hindrance to a career. Yet this shared fear is hardly imaginary. Aon’s Voice of Women Study 2024 , India , which surveyed over 24,000 women across more than 560 companies, found that 75% of working mothers reported a career setback of one to two years after returning to work. Nearly 40% of these women noted that maternity leaves had led to an adverse impact on their pay; many found their work roles had been altered to positions they did not prefer. Another study published the same year in the Journal of Development Studies revealed that women became 4.3 percentage points less likely to be employed as regular salaried workers at establishments covered by such progressive policies. A statutory measure designed to protect women could, in the absence of adequate safeguards, reinforce employers’ incentives to discriminate. Significantly, the court noted that neither the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, nor the Code on Social Security, 2020, expressly provides a comprehensive framework for post-maternity reintegration of women employees. Stronger and wider enforcement of the policy, transparent post-maternity reintegration measures and accountability for discriminatory attitudes by institutions are the need of the hour.

editorials.title: Party appeal vs candidate risk
editorials.passage:
While others were getting worked up over a former finance secretary’s mischievous pronouncement on the latest GDP figures, I was reading a post by someone altogether more responsible: the Nobel winner Paul Krugman on the US bond market.

He was discussing it with another professor from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. At one point they discussed what happened with, and to, the highly risky, subprime loans.

Krugman mentioned something called copulas, a term I had not heard of. So I googled it and was told that “a copula describes the dependence structure between variables, rather than just the probability of independent events” and further that it “connects individual (marginal) probabilities into a combined picture.”

What does this mean? According to Abe Sklar’s Theorem, which I had not heard of either, “any joint distribution splits into two pieces: the individual behaviors (marginals) and the dependence between them (the copula).”

Further googling, which is the current term for research, showed that copulas were massively used in the programmes used in the financial markets in the West in the period leading up to the crisis of 2008 to model joint risks and extreme events. They might have caused it eventually.

To simplify hugely, for which my apologies, that’s basically what bundling of risky assets was all about. You combined various probabilities and got a single risk probability for the entire package.

The method used was something called a ‘Gaussian copula’. Google told me it “combines different probability distributions into a single joint distribution by capturing the correlation between variables.”

But there was a problem which was ignored: what if there were a few probabilities that were way off the mean? And that’s exactly what happened by September 2008. The whole thing collapsed and we got the Atlantic Financial Crisis whose effects are still being felt.

I will not stretch the analogy too far because that would be ridiculous. But it occurred to me that the question of joint probabilities could be important in the context of politics also because political parties combine the risks in individual candidates and come up with consolidated assessments of their chances of winning X or Y or Z number of seats, a kind of Gaussian copula, if you like.

The BJP for example believes that, as a party, it can definitely win between 220-240 seats. That’s like a normal distribution with most of its candidates falling under the bell. But what of the tails of this distribution?

This can become of critical importance if there are too many candidates with extreme risks. They would lie at the tails of the distribution. It is easy to get an idea of their riskiness by looking at the winning and losing margins.

So consider: of the 543 candidates chosen to contest an election, even if 20 per cent fall in this category, where the margins are small, the BJP could lose nearly 108 seats. Something like that may well have happened in 2024 when it lost 63 seats, of which 33 were in UP. Poor candidate selection, rather than any lofty reason like the rumoured abolition of reservations, could have been the reason.

The same thing applies to all political parties. They all can, and do, choose candidates with high risks of losing for whatever local reason.

The Congress is a case in point and it should look into this if it wants to increase its Lok Sabha strength. Is it choosing its candidates badly? In Gaussian terms, is the tail demolishing the dog?

Back in 2014, Rahul Gandhi tried to reform the ticket distribution method by choosing candidates via the American primaries process, which is basically “may the most popular person get the ticket”. It was a great initiative because it sought to minimise tail risk.

But it failed spectacularly. The Congress went from 207 seats in 2009 to just 44 in 2014. There are many theories about why this happened but no one questions either the need or the method used to minimise candidate risk. Rahul then gave up the reform.

A very popular party leader like Indira Gandhi or Narendra Modi can be used to mitigate some of the high risk. People then vote for that leader rather than the candidate.

The problem lies, however, in (a) the popular leader no longer being able to mitigate the risk sufficiently and (b) in choosing too many high-risk candidates, hoping for the best. This is why at least a quarter or more of all contestants always lose.

So the real task is to identify and accept high tail risk. This becomes hard when there is competition within a party to distribute patronage because tail risks get underestimated and are reported wrongly to the party high commands.

Published on September 7, 2026

editorials.title: Ways to deal with FCNR liquidity deluge
editorials.passage:
The deluge of forex into the country on account of the FCNR/OFCB/ECB scheme has been a blessing. It raises the forex reserves, which in turn looks healthier in terms of import cover. It adds to liquidity in a big way such that there is discussion on how to deal with surpluses.

The final number after the non-FCNR flows are reckoned could well cross $150 billion after the announced $137 billion garnered so far. What does it mean to all the parties concerned?

For the RBI, the inflow of $137 billion means approximately 20 per cent increase in reserves from the level of $682 billion as of June 5. This can be used for several purposes. First, it can be used for spot interventions in the market as and when required. Second, it can be used to square off forwards books which stood at $103 billion as of June 30. Third, it can be invested in US treasuries or any other asset as per the policy being pursued. There could be a return of 4.7-5 per cent on these investments depending on the tenure of investment.

There is, however, also a swap cost for the central banks which can be around 3 per cent. With a round ₹13 lakh crore being given to banks for the swap of $137 billion, there can be a cost of ₹39,000 crore on an annual basis. This will however be covered by the investments in US treasuries, thus giving a positive net return. This will be positive for the income and expenditure statement.

On the other hand, given a larger balance sheet, the contingency buffer to be maintained increases in value terms, which can counter this increase in revenue. Also, if the RBI sells its holdings of GSec to manage liquidity then the interest earned from them would come down. Hence it needs to be seen if the surplus to the government can be maintained under ceteris paribus conditions.

For banks, the issues will be different. They have procured clean funds at the cost of 6.25-7.25 per cent for five years. This higher amount of ₹13 lakh crore in dollar terms would entail an interest outgo of say ₹87,750 crore. The swap cost of hedging this interest at 3 per cent would be around ₹2,600 crore as this is not covered by the central bank. Now these funds have to be deployed in either lending or investments. Presently the weighted average lending rate on loans is 8.52 per cent for all banks, which means that there can be a spread of about 1.75 per cent, assuming average cost of 6.75 per cent.

The surplus of ₹13 lakh crore in the system has implications for the markets. These funds would be used to manage the loan book without seeking recourse to bulk deposits or certificates of deposits. Hence these two markets will get depressed.

Increasing the CRR through an incremental CRR may not be fair for banks which have not been aggressive in collecting such deposits. MSS issuance is a way out which can be used to support the fiscal deficit thus obviating the need for fresh borrowing. OMOs are also likely where RBI sells its holding of government paper. The last is VRRR on a rolling basis — which will be an inferior solution for banks as the returns are the lowest.

Curiously, markets have been quite unmoved with the bond yields remaining where they are with expectations of a rate hike in future. The rupee has strengthened now, more out of sentiment. The dollars garnered will not directly affect the market as long as they are used to build reserves. If they are sold in the market, then it will help to strengthen the rupee.

The scheme raises some interesting ideas for further discussion. First, should the FCNR scheme be used periodically whenever it is felt that there is some slippage in the forex reserves? Based on the way in which the scheme was started and terminated early due to its success, a target sum can be announced such that the swap cost taken on by the RBI is, say, $50 billion. Once this level is reached, the scheme can be stopped.The RBI can ask other central banks to invest in bonds issued by Indian banks in dollars, guaranteed by RBI, with a higher return than offered by the Fed. The protocol can be akin to FCNR, with similar spin-offs.

The writer is Chief Economist, Bank of Baroda. Views are personal

Published on September 7, 2026

editorials.title: Innovation with a purpose
editorials.passage: By Arjun Malhotra In recent years, we have witnessed a rapid switch towards digitisation and greater innovation in all sectors. India now proudly stands as a beacon in digital public infrastructure (DPI), with nations looking to emulate our advancements in creating seamless, paperless, and cashless protocols. This fusion of physical and digital, or ‘phygital’ infrastructure, coupled with our vast demographics and growing demand, is expected to give India a 5-6% growth rate at a time when the global economy is pegged at around 3-4%. ALSO READA liquidity mismatch for CAS As the world's most populous nation, India must move beyond being the back office of global economies. The path to becoming a high-income nation lies in indigenisation, sustainable innovation and creating high-value jobs through products that are designed and made in India. This will require a shift in mindset - from assembling products developed elsewhere to building capabilities across the entire value chain, including design, engineering, manufacturing and after-sales support. It's important that our products are localised, with little or no reliance on foreign components. At every step of the journey, we also need to innovate. In the 1970s, for example, when we had no UPS systems and were plagued by frequent power cuts, at HCL we designed power shutoff auto restart (PSAR) systems, to enable seamless workflows. To tweak our products to address our unique challenges, we need to deepen our R&D and think more about hardware innovations. This is important because we need to make products tailored to our needs, meeting specific functionality and safety requirements, and price points. Innovation should not be limited to adding more features; it should focus on solving problems that are specific to Indian conditions, whether they relate to affordability, infrastructure constraints, climate or ease of use. Our products must also be easily repairable to minimise environmental impact and foster inclusive growth. By designing Make in India, low-cost products, we will be able to address the mismatch in digital accessibility. The India consumer electronics market size was valued at $73.73 billion in 2022 and is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.8% from 2023 to 2030. Therefore, India needs to rapidly transform into a manufacturing hub for new-generation electronics products with minimal dependence on foreign components. Designing and manufacturing in India will also safeguard us from external threats, such as covert spyware embedded within electronic hardware. Hidden vulnerabilities in cheap foreign products may lead to cyber-attacks, jeopardising our government institutions, banking systems, defence systems, energy sectors, and even our space programmes. Hardware vulnerabilities pose even greater risks than software. Thus, the local is also safe. Think of the huge data that can be generated by digitising records of ASHA workers, who are ensuring last-mile healthcare delivery. There is one ASHA worker for every 1000-2500 population. Digital accessibility of ASHA workers, with cheap quality tablets, for instance, will significantly transform healthcare delivery. ALSO READInside Track by Coomi Kapoor: Outsiders unwelcome Similarly, there is a huge ground we can cover in education and employment by ensuring our products are not expensive. Make in India products thus fire all cylinders in one go - development, inclusivity, growth, and safety. The writer is co-founder, HCL and chairperson EPIC Foundation Disclaimer: The views expressed are the author's own and do not reflect the official policy or position of Financial Express.

editorials.title: I had an amazing experience as a disabled person at school in the 70s. Since then, discrimination has got far worse
editorials.passage:
A s a disabled person, you’re forced to repeatedly explain your medical history – but for this article, I think it’s important. I was born with a very rare type of cancer called a neuroblastoma. In 1965, it was pretty much a death sentence. Luckily, I took part in a clinical trial and, with only days to live, I had major surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy with a new drug. Despite being given no more than five years to live, on my last birthday I celebrated hitting 60. I doubt anyone in 1965 would have imagined how attitudes towards disabled people would improve as I grew up. It is devastating to see how those same attitudes have reversed in the past decade or two.

The cancer left me with a paralysed right leg, so I wore a leg brace, but otherwise I was a pretty normal kid. I was lucky to be starting school in 1970 when the Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act came into force, which made it possible for disabled children to attend mainstream schools, if they could manage it. My parents moved across Luton to be near the only school that would accept me on a trial run and then as a pupil. When I was a child, if you could manage living like non-disabled people then you were allowed to do so. Not the fully inclusive practice I later campaigned for, but an acknowledgment that disabled people shouldn’t be written off.

At 15, my spine collapsed and crushed the nerves to both legs, an unforeseen side effect of chemo. After months in hospital I came home a full-time wheelchair user. I was lucky our town centre in Luton was very wheelchair accessible and, during my time in hospital, my high school put in some serious adaptations to ensure I could return. Accessible toilets and a lift meant I could take my exams without any real difficulty, thanks to Putteridge high school and the then headteacher, Mr Price. At Luton sixth form college, adaptations were made again, this time under my guidance. Through the course of my childhood ideas around disability had changed from “if they can, let them try” to “what can we do to help them succeed?” and even “what do they want us to do?”

That was the overarching attitude I encountered for the next 20 years. Some viewed being disabled as a tragedy, others as part of life. Most people saw any help that we received as important and something a healthy society should be offering. The exception was the workplace. I tried two jobs, both of which ended in me being sacked because I took a couple of days off. One was because I broke my foot in a lift that was too small for my wheelchair, the other was following a car accident. Both times, taking sick leave was seen as proof that disabled people couldn’t manage the world of work. So I focused on my hobby, music, and was soon touring the UK and Europe playing in bands. This led to my discovery by a TV producer. I ended up on the BBC, ITV and Channel 4, where my show Beat That won an Emmy. My media career, as one of the first disabled celebrities, lasted more than 15 years and only ended during a period of ill health.

In the late 90s and early 00s, I found attitudes became twisted towards an angrier, almost jealous view of disabled people. My Motability vehicle was vandalised repeatedly, because local people were upset about my “free car”. This morphed into “free car, free house and loads of benefits” as Tony Blair’s government, from 1998 onwards, implemented cuts to the benefits bill that scapegoated disabled people. I was attacked twice, my car was vandalised every week and my wife was beaten to a pulp by three people wearing masks. When they threatened to burn our flat down, we packed up and left our fully adapted home to rent somewhere that was safe from violence but totally unsuitable. The police? Useless.

My own brother even once spouted that it was “all right for you with your free car, free house and benefits cash”. It was especially galling as I had worked most of my adult life, paying taxes. The only time I stopped work was when I was very ill. My wife cared for me during this time, and we went from earning about £50,000 in joint income to being paid £15,000 in benefits to cover everything, including our rent. Luckily I got well again, retrained and went back to work as an access consultant.

But those toxic narratives seem to be getting worse, and have become embedded in the national psyche. Successive governments and the media have continued to tell the public lies, such as the much repeated accusations of huge amounts of fraud within the so-called “disability benefits” system that has led to terrifying levels of anger. Only a week ago I was punched in the street for being a “scrounger”.

I call them lies because that’s what they are. Motability is not a free car. It is a vehicle that is leased for a set fee over a three- or five-year period. We don’t get a free Mercedes or BMW. We make a huge upfront payment and it costs the same per week as a tiny little car. And personal independence payment (Pip) is not an out-of-work benefit. It is paid to support independent living, based on people’s ability and support needs. No one is getting it for tennis elbow. In fact, Pip and its forerunners allowed me to work, and my Motability vehicle lets me travel the UK working as co-CEO of the national charity Phab . The access to work scheme saves employers money by paying towards the adaptations and support a disabled worker might need. It brings in £1.48 for every £1 paid out, with the wider economy benefiting by £3.86, according to research carried out by the Royal National Institute of Blind People.

As we mark 31 years since the Disability Discrimination Act and 16 since that was superseded by the Equality Act, please don’t believe the hype around disabled people. Try to imagine a day walking in our shoes, or pushing our wheels. Before you allow the hype around “the freebies” we get, do some research. My wheelchair alone cost me £6,500, for example. No support; that was all out of my pocket.

As I visit the clubs and events Phab supports I meet many disabled people who can only dream of having a life like mine. But shouldn’t all disabled people have the chance to shine? When I was young I had hoped that the future would allow disabled people to fulfil their potential, and let them lead the discussion around making society more accessible and inclusive for everyone. An accessible, inclusive society helps us all. Take the lift, the ability to text and voice-to-text software. All designed to help disabled people, but now a boon to us all. If disabled people are listened to, everyone benefits.

I doubt many of us considered that things would get worse, but if disabled people are allowed to tell the reality of our lives maybe we can get back to a positive place. One where being disabled is just part of daily life. Not sad or tragic, or a licence for free government handouts. Just normal.

Mik Scarlet is co-CEO of the national charity Phab , a campaigner and a music journalist for Blitzed magazine

editorials.title: Israeli ministers keep telling everyone their brutal plans – so why doesn’t the world take them seriously?
editorials.passage:
T he gap between what is being inflicted on Palestinians and the appropriate reaction on the part of the international community has always been vast. But now it yawns so wide that it swallows reality itself. As arms export licences for Israel from states such as Germany surge , talk of harsher measures and sanctions on the part of other European countries remains talk . People continue to be killed in Gaza, Palestinian families remain besieged in the West Bank, and the Israeli political right has been removing all doubt that these violations are intentional, by telling the world of its hopes and plans.

A sample from only the past few days. On Thursday, Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, detailed a scheme for the illegal ethnic cleansing of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip. He also posted an AI-generated video, now deleted, of Palestinian men entering a conveyor belt into detention, emerging emaciated and tearful. Also a few days ago, the defence minister, Israel Katz, stated that the country was “ organised and prepared ” to expel Palestinians from Gaza “by every way possible”.

This macabre theatre continues to unfold, its performances less plausible by the day. The Board of Peace promises Gaza will be “ redeveloped for the benefit ” of its people, while the notion that those same Palestinians in Gaza cannot be allowed to thrive is expressed by Israeli politicians with consistency and a frequency that makes a mockery of the declarations. Last month, the former head of Israel’s national security council, Giora Eiland, pointed out the fact that Israel’s acceptance of Donald Trump’s 15-point plan was a matter of temporary military tactics, rather than long-term peace. “Israel has no interest in Gaza being rebuilt, it’s better for us that it be destroyed for generations to come,” he said .

Moshe Feiglin, previously a “ far-right outcast ” according to the Times of Israel, is now within reach of a cabinet position as a result of an alliance with the finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist party. In a recent interview, Feiglin said that those who didn’t want to leave Gaza should be compelled to by “every way possible. We’ll shut off his water pipes, for example.”

This sort of talk, from within the very ranks of government, is often dismissed as unrepresentative of the Israeli state and, as there are elections ahead, is written off as the lurid but ultimately unserious rhetoric of electioneering. But people such as Ben-Gvir and Katz are not fringe voices, they are ministers with high-impact executive briefs – security and defence – that they have indeed used to push policy that matches their statements.

Ben-Gvir has reopened the underground Rakefet prison , one closed in the 1980s for being inhumane. He has successfully pushed for the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of terror attacks, and celebrated the legislation with a noose-themed cake. Torture and sexual abuse in Israeli prisons are widely documented, the latter earning Israel a spot on the UN’s sexual violence in war zones blacklist. As Ben-Gvir himself is fond of saying, “ we promised, we delivered ”.

Katz has approved the biggest settlement expansion in the West Bank in decades and justified the move on the grounds that it “prevents the establishment of a Palestinian state that would endanger Israel”; he recently advanced legalisation of outpost settlement farms in the West Bank, and instructed the IDF to hand over law enforcement in the West Bank to the Israeli police , which is a stealth move towards annexation.

As the Knesset member Ahmad Tibi wrote in Haaretz earlier this year, a fiction exists at the heart of Israeli politics, where politicians’ efforts to explain and justify policy to international opinion proceed as though “the racism and extremism now driving government policy exist only on the margins”. When really, it lies at the heart of the state.

And if some of the more extreme statements are just electioneering, what does that say about the parameters of discourse in the country if your campaign is mass ethnic cleansing? What does that say about not only the future of Gaza, but all Palestinians in occupied territories who are labouring under home demolitions , militant settlers and the de facto annexation of the West Bank?

Even if these figures are a minority, both in terms of the seats held in the Knesset and the relative number of people who have voted for them, they still hold the levers of power, there is no substantial domestic mobilisation against them, and the rest of the system is unable or unwilling to stop them. The distinctions around how big their constituency may be or how representative they are of Israelis in general matters not a jot to the fate of Palestinians over whom they have been given executive dominion.

The question now is, why are these people not being taken at their word? Why is there no sense of urgency and outrage. Why are these policies and stated goals from the Israeli state not taken seriously and met with appropriate sanctions, trade and arms embargos, and international censure? There is a wild asymmetry when it comes to the perceived potency of Israeli rhetoric and action. “From the river to sea”, for example, as expressed by Palestinians and their supporters has become stigmatised and its use censured. But the most extreme interpretation of that phrase, that it means only one sovereign people in the mentioned land, is commonplace in Israel.

The founding charter of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party states that “between the sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty”. Netanyahu himself last week attended a gathering at a religious-Zionist yeshiva, nodding along to a Kahanist song belted out by the attenders. “Remember me, please, give me strength just this time, O God, to take revenge, if only for one of my two eyes, on Palestine,” they sang, adding “May their name be erased!” “There are no more red lines,” was how a Haaretz writer described the scene.

The international community has averted its eyes as red lines are trampled over. This can only be a combination of cowardice and acceptance, barely obscured by feeble statements of condemnation here and there, and grounded in the belief or resignation that Palestinian lives shall be consigned to hell. The facts are clear and plentiful. The Israeli right has a plan and a sense of direction, one that it has nursed for a very long time, and now given nourishment by the 7 October attacks.

Some may not be realisable (ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza is limited by the fact there are no countries that can or will receive them), but much of it is. The direction of travel is clear and there have been some huge successes so far. There is a line connecting the hundreds of thousands of Palestinians expelled or forced to flee in 1948 and today. The security and carceral state that Palestinians exist in, the destruction of their homes and infrastructure, the settlement and fracturing of their territories, and the extension of Israeli sovereignty over them in ways that dehumanise and oppress, all serve to ensure that a future in which Palestinians are free, let alone thriving in self-governance, never emerges.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Lindsay Clancy’s case is a rorschach test
editorials.passage:
M ost family annihilators are men. It’s a grim fact that such incidents are common enough to have a discernible pattern. The massacre is carried out by a husband and father, often one who is on the verge of bankruptcy or divorce ; typically, it forms the finale of a long reign of domestic violence terror.

About half the time , the perpetrator kills himself after slaughtering his family. Gun use is common – a large number of what are termed “mass shootings” in the United States are in fact family annihilation killings, in which a man turns his weapon on his family members. Other times, the killer uses knives, or fires.

This kind of killing does not always make the news. When it does, news organizations often run family photos, in which the killer smiles on a beach or beside the Grand Canyon with his arm around the wife and children he will later shoot or strangle.

In this context of pervasive and normalized male domestic violence against women and children, the Lindsay Clancy case was always going to attract outside attention. Because in that case, when three Massachusetts children were strangled of their family home in January of 2023 – Cora, who was five, Dawson, who was three, and Callan, who was just eight months old – the killer was their mom.

As is fairly common for family annihilators, Clancy attempted suicide after killing her children. But Clancy survived. Injuries left her paralyzed below the waist. At her murder trial, which lasted an unusually long six weeks and concluded in a hung jury on Friday, she rolled to the defense table each morning in a wheelchair.

The mistrial means that Clancy – along with her children’s father, their grandparents, and everyone else who loved them, to say nothing of the state – will now face the possibility of being subjected to a second trial. All because of a hung jury.

Eleven of the 12 jurors accepted the argument put forward by Clancy’s defense, that Clancy, who does not contest that she killed her children, was suffering from an acute case of postpartum psychosis , and hence could not be held legally responsible for their deaths. But according to notes that the forewoman of the jury sent to the judge, one juror, a man, expressed “reasonable doubt” about Clancy’s culpability under the law, but refused to apply that doubt as is legally required.

That this lone juror who wanted to convict Clancy was male is relevant, because the Clancy case itself became, in the distorting ways that such stories tend to when they are witnessed en masse through social media, a referendum on motherhood, mental healthcare, and the status of women.

Some mothers have expressed deep sympathy for Clancy’s postpartum mental health crises, citing resonances with their own experiences and a hope that the case can bring greater attention to the rare but acute and debilitating kind of postpartum mental suffering that Clancy seems to have experienced; others say that medical neglect of the condition, and of the experiences of postpartum women more broadly, create the conditions for tragedies like that of the Clancy family.

Some on the misogynist right, meanwhile, have seized upon Clancy’s actions and the support she has received as evidence that women are congenitally evil, disposed to violence, untrustworthy, and unfit for public life.

Your opinion on the Clancy case will likely largely depend on whether you believe her defense team’s claim that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis that was severe enough that she experienced the kind of delusions, hallucinations, paranoia, rapid shifts in mood, and other departures from reality that would render her not responsible for her own actions. In other words, do you think she was really ill , or do you think that she killed her children in cold blood, and is lying?

The facts suggest that she isn’t. Clancy had a history of postpartum psychological distress following the births of her first two children, in 2017 and 2019. She was prescribed medication after those births, and seems to have been a loving and attentive mother to them for years.

But following the birth of her third child, a little boy named Callan, in 2022, reports suggest that Clancy began to experience something different, and much more serious, than her previous bouts with postpartum anxiety.

She couldn’t sleep, wasn’t eating, and would experience bouts of sudden, acute terror. Going back to her job as a nurse in a labor and delivery unit seemed impossible; she could barely function. She sought help again and was diagnosed with anxiety.

Later, she would speak to other mental health practitioners, too. A series of providers issued her a stunning array of psychiatric medications. As her sleeplessness continued, Clancy was prescribed increasingly powerful tranquilizers.

More than a month before she killed her children, Clancy reported that she had begun to hallucinate. She kept seeking help, saying that she was thinking of killing herself; she told both her mother and her husband that she feared she would harm her children, though she had never mistreated them before.

Clancy briefly checked herself in to inpatient treatment, but left after just a few nights. The Clancys seem to have thought that longer-term hospitalization was out of the question. After all, she had kids to take care of. Soon, she was hearing voices.

Those who are most outraged by the Clancy case, and by the sympathy that a homicidal mother has received, are disturbed by the unnaturalness of a woman killing her children, disturbed by what they fear is a secret core of hate and depravity in women that could be unleashed at any time.

But if I were a psychoanalyst, I might say that the right wing that imagines all women as potential Lindsay Clancys is projecting their own guilt: on some level, they know that what our culture asks mothers to do is unsustainable, cruel, and often quite literally maddening.

Because to me, what is most haunting about the Clancy case is how ordinary and unsurprising all the failures were that led to her break.

She was failed in ordinary ways by providers who saw a woman living in relative comfort and assumed her suffering could not be very serious; she was failed in ordinary ways by a community that understands motherhood to be a state of variously mild and acute suffering, and has so normalized women’s disappearance into the family that they can barely see the mother for the baby.

She was failed by the expectation that women will persevere through their own suffering, even their most disturbing and agonizing moments, to care for their children; she was failed by the trivialization of women’s lives, and by the blithe assumption that the so-called “baby blues” were mere neurotic episodes, not psychotic breaks requiring serious clinical interventions. Her children were failed, too.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist
